grades.quote: A runnable thread that has been patiently waiting for the CPU, on the other hand, retains a fixed virtual runtime. As such, it will eventually have the lowest virtual runtime, and hence will be chosen to run (once a thread switch occurs).
grades.reason: Describes Linux's proportional-share (virtual runtime) scheduler, not a decay-usage scheduler. It does explain a related idea: a thread that waited keeps a low virtual runtime and eventually gets chosen, while recent CPU use pushes threads later on the timeline. That is only loosely relevant to the decay-usage question.
Chapter introduction and roadmap for scheduling. It says nothing about decay-usage priority adjustment or why a waking thread is favored.

grades.quote: One advantage to decreasing the priority of running processes below the base, as in Mac OS X, rather than only down to the base, as in Microsoft Windows, is that doing so will normally prevent any runnable thread from being permanently ignored
grades.reason: This passage is from the decay-usage scheduling section. It touches on lowering the priority of running threads, usage decay factors, and a priority boost after waiting for keyboard input. It does not directly explain why recent CPU usage makes a waking thread win. It focuses on starvation avoidance and on tuned magic numbers, so it gives only auxiliary context.
